subject: Career
title: The Network Audit: Mapping Your Gaps
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Network Audit: Mapping Your Gaps.

hook.text: She drew her network on paper. Everyone was in her department. Her entire network was one color.

buildup.text: A network audit maps your connections by type: industry, function, seniority, and geography.

discovery.text: Gaps in your network are blind spots in your career. No finance contacts means no financial perspective.

twist.text: Most people's networks are 80% similar to themselves. Homophily — we connect with people like us.

climax.text: Audit annually: list your top 20 contacts. Map them by category. Fill the gaps intentionally.

punchline.text: You can't see what your network can't show you. Map the gaps.

quiz.question: What is homophily in networking?
options: The tendency to connect with people similar to ourselves

details.summary: Mapping network gaps reveals which industries, seniority levels, functions, and geographies are underrepresented in your professional relationships. These gaps directly correspond to blind spots in your career intelligence and opportunity pipeline.
details.whyItMatters: Network gaps are invisible threats to career growth. You do not know what you are missing until you systematically map what is absent from your professional constellation.
takeaways: Common gaps include senior leadership contacts and cross-industry ties
Geographic gaps limit awareness of opportunities in other markets
Fill the most strategically important gaps first rather than all at once

faq.question: What are the most common network gaps professionals overlook?
faq.answer: Upward gaps, meaning lack of connections to people two or more levels above, are the most common and costly. Cross-functional gaps, where you only know people in your own department, and industry gaps that limit your view of adjacent opportunities are also frequently overlooked.

faq.question: How do you prioritize which network gaps to fill first?
faq.answer: Align gap-filling with your career goals. If you want a promotion, prioritize senior contacts. If you are considering a career change, prioritize cross-industry ties. If you want to innovate, prioritize contacts from completely different disciplines.
